🗂️ Text and JSON File Storage in TypeScript

Small TypeScript projects often do not need a full database. A text file or JSON file can be enough for local storage, basic persistence, prototypes, classroom projects, or command-line tools. The main idea is simple: read the file into memory, update the data, and write the file back out.

When This Approach Makes Sense

  • Small projects with a limited amount of data
  • Practice projects and classroom assignments
  • Local tools used by one person at a time
  • Simple prototypes before moving to a real database

If many users need to access the same data at the same time, or if the data becomes large and complex, a real database is usually the better tool.

Use the fs Module

Node.js includes the fs module for reading and writing files. In modern TypeScript projects, the promise-based API is the easiest option because it works cleanly with async and await.

Example: Import Promise-Based File Tools

import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";

Reading and Writing a Text File

A plain text file works well when you just need to store notes, logs, or a list of strings.

Example: Save and Load Text Data

import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";

async function saveNote(note: string): Promise<void> {
  await writeFile("notes.txt", note, "utf-8");
}

async function loadNote(): Promise<string> {
  return readFile("notes.txt", "utf-8");
}

In this example, the file acts like a storage container. You write data into it, and later read that data back into your program.

Reading and Writing JSON Like a Tiny Database

JSON is often a better option because it can store structured data. For example, you can keep an array of users, tasks, quiz scores, or inventory items.

Example: Types for JSON Data

type StudentRecord = {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  grade: number;
};

Example: Read and Write JSON Records

import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";

type StudentRecord = {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  grade: number;
};

const filePath = "students.json";

async function readStudents(): Promise<StudentRecord[]> {
  const fileContents = await readFile(filePath, "utf-8");
  return JSON.parse(fileContents) as StudentRecord[];
}

async function writeStudents(students: StudentRecord[]): Promise<void> {
  const json = JSON.stringify(students, null, 2);
  await writeFile(filePath, json, "utf-8");
}

Adding a New Record

The usual pattern is read, update in memory, then write the updated data back to the file.

Example: Insert a Record

async function addStudent(newStudent: StudentRecord): Promise<void> {
  const students = await readStudents();
  students.push(newStudent);
  await writeStudents(students);
}

Updating or Deleting a Record

Example: Update and Delete

async function updateStudentGrade(
  id: number,
  newGrade: number,
): Promise<void> {
  const students = await readStudents();
  const updatedStudents = students.map((student) =>
    student.id === id ? { ...student, grade: newGrade } : student,
  );

  await writeStudents(updatedStudents);
}

async function deleteStudent(id: number): Promise<void> {
  const students = await readStudents();
  const filteredStudents = students.filter((student) => student.id !== id);
  await writeStudents(filteredStudents);
}

Handling a Missing File

A common problem is that the file does not exist yet. You can catch that error and return a sensible default, such as an empty array.

Example: Safe JSON Read

async function readStudentsSafe(): Promise<StudentRecord[]> {
  try {
    const fileContents = await readFile(filePath, "utf-8");
    return JSON.parse(fileContents) as StudentRecord[];
  } catch (error) {
    return [];
  }
}

💡 Why This Works

Treat the file as persistent storage, but do the actual data work in TypeScript using arrays, objects, and functions. That is what makes it feel similar to a tiny database.

Important Limits

⚠️ Be Careful About

  • Two writes at the same time can overwrite each other if you are not careful
  • Large files become slow because the whole file is often read and rewritten
  • JSON files can break if invalid JSON is written into them
  • This approach is best for simple local data, not high-traffic production systems

Example Project Structure

Suggested Layout

my-project/
  src/
    app.ts
    storage.ts
  data/
    students.json
    notes.txt

Quick Start

Install and Run

npm install typescript ts-node --save-dev
npm install @types/node --save-dev

# Run your file-based storage script
npx ts-node src/storage.ts
